ctx.x: Yeah. A lot of times, a lot of times, the bass was lost in a lot of recordings. Yeah. The fidelity of the mixing. So, uh, so we could say, maybe people look at all the instruments. We said the guitar was basically a rhythm instrument in New Orleans music. The bass and the drums, uh, carry the rhythm. And, uh, the horns, it seems the horns and the piano were basically the solo instruments. Yeah. And, uh, did, took care of most of the solos. Yeah. Um. Whereas in, in other parts of the country, Chicago, the guitar…

Uh, down here, there's another thing. And, and I think Sue was producing that, you know, it depends, you know. Because, uh, the producers, Sue, uh, had a gear for music or something, they did pretty well. You know, like I did with Alton, you know. Like they would be able to hear. And they would more guitar and Dave stuff with Imperial than any other label around here. You know, you know, because, many of the recordings, you will notice Imperial, you know. But, uh, other labels, because like I said, that phrase…
When record companies would come from Montana in the 1950s, and people would hear, tell me that story about how people would come to the studio to audition. What the audition process was?
